446 U.S. 740.name: Walker v. Armco Steel Corp.
446 U.S. 740.summary: In this diversity action, Oklahoma law required timely service to stop the limitations period. Filing the complaint under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 3 did not stop that clock. The claim was therefore untimely.

41 U.S. 1.name: Swift v. Tyson
41 U.S. 1.summary: The Court treated a preexisting debt as value for a negotiable bill and allowed a federal court to decide that question of general commercial law independently of state judicial decisions. Erie Railroad Co. v. Tompkins overruled the general-common-law rule in 1938.

505 U.S. 763.name: Two Pesos, Inc. v. Taco Cabana, Inc.
505 U.S. 763.summary: A restaurant could protect its inherently distinctive trade dress under § 43(a) of the Lanham Act without separately proving that customers had learned to associate the design with a single source.

517 U.S. 370.name: Markman v. Westview Instruments, Inc.
517 U.S. 370.summary: The judge determines what a patent claim means, including the meaning of technical terms in the claim. The Seventh Amendment does not give the jury that task in a patent infringement trial.

369 U.S. 469.name: Dairy Queen, Inc. v. Wood
369 U.S. 469.summary: A demand for money for breach of contract or trademark infringement presented legal issues that the defendant could have a jury decide. Calling the demand an accounting and seeking an injunction in the same suit did not eliminate that right.

526 U.S. 687.name: City of Monterey v. Del Monte Dunes at Monterey, Ltd.
526 U.S. 687.summary: The developer was entitled to a jury trial on its § 1983 claim for damages for a regulatory taking. Given the instructions the city accepted and the contested facts surrounding its repeated rejection of development proposals, the issues were properly submitted to the jury.

456 U.S. 273.name: Pullman-Standard v. Swint
456 U.S. 273.summary: Whether a seniority system was adopted with discriminatory intent was a factual finding subject to clear-error review under Rule 52(a). An appellate court could not decide the issue afresh simply by calling intent an ultimate fact.

543 U.S. 111.name: KP Permanent Make-Up, Inc. v. Lasting Impression I, Inc.
543 U.S. 111.summary: A defendant asserting statutory fair use of a descriptive term need not prove that confusion is unlikely. The plaintiff bears the burden of proving likely confusion, and some possibility of confusion can coexist with fair use.

240 U.S. 403.name: Hanover Star Milling Co. v. Metcalf
240 U.S. 403.summary: Common-law trademark rights arose through use in a market. Earlier use elsewhere did not give a business exclusive rights in a remote market where another business independently adopted the mark in good faith and built its own reputation.

316 U.S. 203.name: Mishawaka Rubber & Woolen Manufacturing Co. v. S. S. Kresge Co.
316 U.S. 203.summary: To recover the infringer’s profits under the governing trademark statute, the owner did not have to identify customers who would otherwise have bought its product. The infringer bore the burden of separating profits attributable to other causes.

487 U.S. 552.name: Pierce v. Underwood
487 U.S. 552.summary: An appellate court reviews for abuse of discretion a trial court’s determination that the government lacked substantial justification under the Equal Access to Justice Act. The government’s position must have a reasonable basis in both law and fact.

363 U.S. 278.name: Commissioner v. Duberstein
363 U.S. 278.summary: Whether a transfer is a gift for federal income-tax purposes turns principally on the transferor’s intent under the circumstances. The Court upheld the Tax Court’s finding that a Cadillac given for business leads was taxable income.

443 U.S. 526.name: Dayton Board of Education v. Brinkman
443 U.S. 526.summary: The Dayton school board had operated an intentionally segregated system and had a continuing duty to remove its effects. Evidence of systemwide violations and their continuing consequences supported a systemwide desegregation remedy.

293 U.S. 474.name: Dimick v. Schiedt
293 U.S. 474.summary: The Seventh Amendment barred a federal judge from increasing a jury’s personal-injury damages award as a condition of denying the plaintiff a new trial, even with the defendant’s consent.

84 U.S. 657.name: Railroad Co. v. Stout
84 U.S. 657.summary: The jury could find the railroad negligent for leaving a turntable accessible to children. Even when the underlying facts are undisputed, jurors may decide negligence if reasonable people could draw different conclusions from those facts.

338 U.S. 338.name: United States v. Yellow Cab Co.
338 U.S. 338.summary: The Court affirmed judgment for the defendants in the government’s antitrust suit. Rule 52’s clear-error standard applied to the government’s appeal, and the trial judge permissibly chose between competing readings of the evidence.

574 U.S. 418.name: Hana Financial, Inc. v. Hana Bank
574 U.S. 418.summary: When a jury trial is requested and the facts are disputed, the jury decides whether an earlier and a later mark create the same continuing commercial impression for ordinary consumers. If they do, the owner can use the earlier mark’s priority date.

575 U.S. 138.name: B&B Hardware, Inc. v. Hargis Industries, Inc.
575 U.S. 138.summary: A Trademark Trial and Appeal Board decision on likelihood of confusion can bind the parties in a later infringement suit when the trademark uses considered by the Board are materially the same and the usual requirements for issue preclusion are satisfied.

583 U.S. 387.name: U.S. Bank National Association v. Village at Lakeridge, LLC
583 U.S. 387.summary: The appeals court properly used clear-error review to assess whether a bankruptcy transaction was conducted at arm’s length under its test for nonstatutory insider status. Applying that test required chiefly factual work.

591 U.S. 549.name: United States Patent and Trademark Office v. Booking.com B.V.
591 U.S. 549.summary: Combining a generic word with .com does not automatically make the resulting mark generic. The question is what consumers understand the entire term to mean. On the facts found below, consumers did not understand Booking.com as the name of a class of services.

599 U.S. 140.name: Jack Daniel’s Properties, Inc. v. VIP Products LLC
599 U.S. 140.summary: When VIP used the challenged design to identify the source of its dog toy, ordinary likelihood-of-confusion analysis applied even though the design parodied Jack Daniel’s. The parody likewise did not automatically exempt that source-identifying use from dilution liability.

529 U.S. 205.name: Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. v. Samara Brothers, Inc.
529 U.S. 205.summary: To protect an unregistered product design as trade dress under § 43(a) of the Lanham Act, the owner must show that consumers have come to associate the design with a particular source. Product design cannot qualify as inherently distinctive.
